::: {.why}
Everybody says returns have fat tails, almost nobody says how fat, and the difference between those two states is whether you can size a position.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Report the standardised size of the largest daily move in your sample and say what probability a normal model assigns to it.
- Say why the sample kurtosis is a bad estimator for this and name what you would report instead.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>55 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Measure: for each of your three series, report the sample skewness and kurtosis, the largest standardised move, the number of moves beyond four standard deviations, and the number a normal model predicts over the same sample length. Put the two counts side by side.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Show the estimator problem: bootstrap the sample kurtosis of SPY returns and plot its distribution. Then compute kurtosis on the first and second half of the sample separately. The instability you see is why practitioners report quantile ratios and tail counts rather than a fourth moment.
:::
:::
